---
title: "1. Getting started"
description: "Install the package, see which data exist and download your first table of deaths by neighborhood."
ordem: 1
tempo: "10 min"
---

## What you need

- **R** (4.1 or newer) and, preferably, **RStudio**.
- An internet connection. The first time, the package downloads IBGE tables (about 340 MB for Rio de Janeiro state). After that they stay on your computer.

## 1. Install

```r
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Hendesson/localdatasus")

# For maps (optional):
install.packages(c("sf", "ggplot2", "leaflet"))
```

After installing, **restart R** (in RStudio: *Session → Restart R*).

## 2. See what exists

Not every place has neighborhood data: only some health departments publish it. Start by asking the package:

```r
library(localdatasus)
onde_tem_bairro()        # "where is there neighborhood data?"
```

The table lists each **dado** (data: deaths, births, dengue, tuberculosis...), the **local** (place), the **unidade** (unit: neighborhood or district) and the **funcao** (the function that fetches it). In short:

| Where | Deaths | Births | Notifiable diseases (SINAN) | Hospitalizations | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rio de Janeiro (city) | ✔ since 2006 | ✔ | ✔ 15 diseases | ✔ | |
| Other municipalities of Rio de Janeiro state | ✔ neighborhoods since 2011 | ✔ (with postal code) | — | ✔ | |
| São Paulo (city) | ✔ by district | ✔ | ✔ 5 diseases | ✔ | |
| Fortaleza | ✔ since 1999 | ✔ | — | ✔ | |
| Recife | — | — | ✔ dengue, chikungunya, zika | ✔ | SAMU |
| Curitiba | — | — | — | ✔ | medical consultations (e-Saúde) |
| Santa Catarina state | — | — | ✔ 6 diseases | ✔ | |
| Other states | — | — | — | ✔ (by postal code) | |

In **every municipality** you can also count **health facilities** (CNES) by neighborhood.

## 3. Your first table

Deaths from **diseases of the circulatory system** (ICD-10 chapter IX, codes starting with **I**) in Rio de Janeiro's neighborhoods, 2023:

```r
circ <- obitos_bairro("Rio de Janeiro", 2023, cid = "I")
#> Pronto: 15.502 obitos em 160 bairros; 99,8% ligados a um bairro do IBGE.
#> (Done: 15,502 deaths in 160 neighborhoods; 99.8% linked to an IBGE neighborhood.)

head(circ)
```

Each row is a neighborhood:

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ano`, `municipio` | year and municipality |
| `bairro` | official IBGE neighborhood name |
| `bairro_no_site` | the name as written in the original source |
| `obitos` | number of deaths |
| `populacao` | neighborhood population (2022 Census) |
| `taxa_por_10mil` | deaths per 10,000 inhabitants |
| `lat`, `lon` | neighborhood coordinates (for maps) |
| `codigo_ibge` | official neighborhood code |
| `ligacao` | how the name was linked to IBGE (`exata` = exact, `parcial` = partial...) |
| `fonte` | where the data came from |

## 4. Sort and save

```r
# Neighborhoods with the highest rate
circ[order(-circ$taxa_por_10mil), c("bairro", "obitos", "taxa_por_10mil")][1:10, ]

# Save as CSV (opens in Excel, QGIS...)
write.csv(circ, "deaths_circulatory_rio_2023.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Write it your way
The municipality name ignores upper/lower case and accents: `"rio de janeiro"`, `"Niteroi"`. You can also use the IBGE code: `"330455"`.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Data are cached
The second time, the same query takes seconds: the package keeps everything in a cache. To clear it, use `limpar_cache()` ("clear cache").
:::
